paragraphs.text: The mouth of the Orange River in south-western Namibia is called the Sperrgebiet, which in German means ‘the forbidden zone’. The area is rich in diamonds, and is therefore one of the world’s most jealously guarded coastlines. Until the 1990s, it was controlled by the mining company De Beers. Today, however, De Beers have shared authority, in partnership with the Namibian government. One day in April 2008, a company geologist came across what looked like a half sphere of rock buried in the beach sands of the Sperrgebiet. He picked it up and immediately realised it was a copper ingot. A trident-shaped mark on its weathered surface turned out to be the hallmark of one of medieval Europe’s wealthiest financiers.

figure.alt: Original map showing Lisbon and Namibia

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists would later find 22 tons of these ingots beneath the sand, along with more than 2,000 beautiful gold coins — mainly Spanish excelentes, but also some Venetian, Moorish, French, and other coinage, including exquisite portugueses bearing the royal coat of arms of Portugal. These are the treasures of what is by far the oldest and richest shipwreck ever found in sub-Saharan Africa. But it is the wreck itself that has really fired the imaginations of the world’s archaeologists. It is a ‘nau’, a classic Portuguese trading ship from the 1530s. The ship is from the heart of the age of discovery, with its cargo of gold, silver, copper and ivory having lain untouched for nearly 500 years.

The story begins on 7th March, 1533, in Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, and the then leading maritime port of Europe. A group of ships sailed grandly down the capital’s Tagus River and into the Atlantic, bound for India, their flags and pennants flying. They were the pride of Portugal, leaving on a voyage of 15 months to bring back precious spices from distant lands. The ships were sturdy and capable, and owned by the king himself. Among them was the Bom Jesus, a brand-new ship captained by Dom Francisco de Noronha, and carrying 300 or so sailors, soldiers, merchants, priests, nobles, and slaves. None of these men would ever return home. It seems that four months or so after their grand departure, the ships were struck and scattered by a huge storm. The account of the voyage by the ships’ commander was lost, and all that remains is a clerk’s acknowledgement of a report that the Bom Jesus had disappeared in wild weather somewhere off southwest Africa. Records show no further indication of the ship’s whereabouts, and its fate remained a mystery until 2008.

Francisco Alves, head of nautical archaeology under the Portuguese Ministry of Culture, says of the Sperrgebiet find: ‘This is a priceless opportunity. We know so little about these great old ships. This is only the second one ever excavated by archaeologists.’ All the others were robbed by treasure hunters — hardly a risk on a coast as tightly guarded as the Sperrgebiet. But pinning a name and a story to a shipwreck found on a far-flung shore is still no easy task — particularly if it is thought to be an early Portuguese wreck. A catastrophic earthquake, tsunami and fire in November 1755 virtually wiped Lisbon off the map, and sent the building that housed the vast majority of precious maps, charts and shipping records tumbling into the Tagus River.

‘That left a huge hole in our history,’ says Alexandre Monteiro, a maritime archaeologist with the Portuguese Ministry of Culture. ‘With the maritime archives gone, one has to revert to other, more imaginative ways of finding information.’ In this instance, a vital clue came from the rare King Joao III portugueses found on the wreck. These were minted for only a few years, from 1525 to 1538, after which they were recalled, melted down, and never reissued. Finding so many sparkling new portugueses is a strong indication that the ship sailed during this 13-year window in time, and that the wreck is indeed the Bom Jesus. Moreover, the load of copper ingots suggests the ship was on its way out to its destination, rather than returning home.

Another intriguing piece of evidence is a letter found in royal archives. Dated February 1533, it reveals that King Joao had just sent a knight to pick up a large amount of gold from a group of Spanish businessmen who had invested in the fleet that was about to sail — the fleet that included the Bom Jesus. Archaeologists had been puzzled by the huge quantity of Spanish coins found among the wreckage — about 70 per cent of the gold pieces were excelentes, unexpected for a Portuguese ship. ‘This letter would go a long way toward explaining that,’ says Monteiro. ‘Spanish investors, it seems, had an unusually large stake in the 1533 fleet.’

And what of the 300 men? Although the discovery of human toe bones in a shoe found among the debris indicates that at least one person did not survive, those were the only human remains recovered from the wreck. And few personal possessions were found on board. These facts led archaeologists to believe that, despite the breakup of the ship along the surf line, many if not most of those aboard made it to land. And then what? It appears that the Sperrgebiet still holds some mysteries that may never be solved.
